title: The Most Ridiculous Wars in History

beats.say: In November 1932, the Australian army rolled into the wheat fields of Western Australia with two machine guns and ten thousand rounds of ammunition.
Their enemy was fast, fearless, about six feet tall, and covered in feathers.
Right, lads. How hard can it be?
Spoiler: very hard.
Today we're counting down six of the most ridiculous wars in history, named after a soup kettle, a bucket, an ear, a pig and, yes, emus.

show.text: The Most Ridiculous Wars in History
show.sub: Six wars. All real. Yes, really.

beats.say: Number six: the Kettle War of 1784.
Antwerp is a port city on the river Scheldt, in what's now Belgium.
But for about two hundred years, the Dutch had kept that river closed to trade ships, which cut Antwerp off from the sea.
By 1784, Antwerp belonged to Austria, and its emperor, Joseph the Second, was sick of it.
It's a river. Rivers are for boats. I'm sending boats.
So he sent ships down the Scheldt, including one called Le Louis, flying the emperor's own flag.
His thinking: surely the Dutch would never dare fire at the emperor's flag.
The Dutch sent out one warship, the Dolfijn.
Stop right there!
Make me.
So the Dolfijn fired.
And according to the story that gave this war its name, the one and only shot hit a soup kettle.
Not the soup!
Le Louis surrendered on the spot.
Joseph did declare war, but France stepped in to calm everyone down.
In a treaty signed in 1785, the river stayed closed, and the Dutch paid the emperor millions of guilders to make it all go away.
Casualties from that one shot: zero people, one kettle, and one lunch.
Number five: the War of the Bucket, northern Italy, 1325.
Modena and Bologna are two cities about twenty-five miles apart, and back then they could not stand each other.
Bologna backed the Pope. Modena backed the Holy Roman Emperor, a powerful German ruler who also claimed northern Italy.
The legend says soldiers from Modena snuck into Bologna and stole a wooden bucket from the town well, and that started a war.
Give us back our bucket!
What bucket?
The real story is a bit different. The real trigger was a castle.
In September 1325, Modena grabbed an important Bolognese castle called Monteveglio.
So in November, Bologna marched out with around thirty-two thousand men, against about seven thousand from Modena.

show.label: Battle of Zappolino, 1325
show.sub: from Bologna, against about 7,000 from Modena

beats.say: Easy win for Bologna, right? Nope.
Modena had professional German soldiers sent by the emperor, while the giant Bolognese army was mostly untrained.
The Bolognese were routed within a couple of hours, and this part was no joke: around two thousand men died.
On the way home, the winners took a bucket from a well just outside Bologna's gates, as a trophy.
We'll just take this, thanks.
And Modena still has it. The original sits in the town hall, and a copy hangs in the city's bell tower.
Number four: the War of Jenkins' Ear. Yes, historians really call it that.
It's 1731, and Robert Jenkins, a British sea captain, is sailing his ship, the Rebecca, home from Jamaica.
A Spanish coast guard ship stops him on suspicion of smuggling, and to be fair, historians say he probably was.

tag.text: Juan de León Fandiño, Spanish captain

beats.say: The Spanish crew roughed him up, and one of them cut off his ear.
Here, take this back to your King George.
Wait, you're giving me my ear back?
Yep. A newspaper report from 1731 says they handed him the piece of his ear and told him to take it to the king.
Jenkins complained to the king's government, and then nothing much happened for seven years.
By 1738, British merchants were furious that Spanish ships kept searching their ships, and politicians who wanted war needed a symbol.
Enter Jenkins' ear.
The famous story says he showed Parliament his ear, pickled in a jar.
Gentlemen, I brought the ear.
Why would you keep it?
Historians doubt the jar scene, but the story spread like wildfire.
Prime Minister Robert Walpole didn't want a war, but the pressure was too much, and in 1739 Britain declared war on Spain.
A war. Over an ear.
And it was not a small war. The biggest British attack, on Cartagena in South America in 1741, was a disaster with heavy losses.
The fighting merged into a much bigger European war, and only formally ended in 1748.
Britain mostly failed to get what it wanted, and the most famous thing about the whole war is still one man's ear.
Number three is the shortest war in recorded history.
Zanzibar is an island off the coast of East Africa.
In 1896, it had its own sultan, or king, but it was a British protectorate, which meant any new sultan needed Britain's approval.
On the twenty-fifth of August, the sultan died suddenly, and Khalid bin Barghash, from the royal family, took the throne without asking.
I'm the sultan now.
Britain wanted someone else, so it sent an ultimatum: leave the palace by nine in the morning on the twenty-seventh, or we open fire.
Leave by nine, or we fire.
You wouldn't dare.
About two thousand eight hundred defenders held the palace, while five British warships lined up in the harbor.
At two minutes past nine, the ships opened fire.
By about twenty to ten, the palace flag had been shot down, and it was over.
The length is the ridiculous part, but the war itself was not a joke.
Around five hundred people on Khalid's side were killed or wounded. On the British side, one sailor was injured.
Khalid escaped to the German consulate, and Britain later made his supporters pay for the shells that had been fired at them.
Number two: the Pig War. And yes, there is a pig.
In 1859, the United States and Britain both claimed San Juan Island, which sits between today's Washington State and Canada.
A treaty said the border ran down the middle of the channel, but there were two channels, and the island sat between them.
On the fifteenth of June 1859, an American farmer named Lyman Cutlar found a pig rooting around in his garden. Again.
Not again!
So he shot it.
The pig belonged to Charles Griffin, who ran a sheep farm on the island for a British company, the Hudson's Bay Company.
Cutlar offered ten dollars. Griffin wanted a hundred.
When British officials threatened to arrest Cutlar, the American settlers asked the U.S. Army for protection.
The Army sent Captain George Pickett with sixty-four soldiers.
Nobody is arresting anybody on this island.
Britain answered with warships, and by the end of August there were four hundred sixty-one American soldiers and fourteen cannons on the island.

show.label: San Juan Island, August 1859
show.sub: US soldiers and 14 cannons, facing British warships with over 2,000 men

beats.say: All over one dead pig.
Luckily, the British admiral in charge, Rear Admiral Robert Baynes, took one look and refused to start shooting.
He told the local governor he would not do this.

show.text: Involve two great nations in a war over a squabble about a pig.

beats.say: Meanwhile, on the island, officers from both sides went to church together and shared whisky and cigars.
The two countries shared the island for twelve years.
Finally, they asked Germany's emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm the First, to settle it, and in 1872 a panel he chose gave the islands to the United States.
Final body count: one pig.
And number one. You knew it was coming. The Great Emu War.
After World War One, Australia gave thousands of ex-soldiers land to farm in Western Australia, often pretty poor land.
Then the Great Depression hit, wheat prices fell, and in 1932 an estimated twenty thousand emus showed up.
Emus are huge birds that can't fly, and these ones found that farms had water and lots of tasty wheat.
Lunch is served, boys.
Many farmers were ex-soldiers, and they knew what works against a big advancing army: machine guns.
Minister, we need machine guns.
For the birds?
For the birds.
Defence Minister Sir George Pearce said yes.
So the army sent Major Meredith, two soldiers, two Lewis machine guns and ten thousand rounds of ammunition.
They even brought along a cameraman to film the big victory.
It began on the second of November. Settlers tried to herd the first flock toward the guns, but the emus split up and ran in every direction.
Why won't they stay in formation?
Two days later, more than a thousand emus came heading straight for an ambush near a dam.
The gunners waited until the birds were close, and opened fire. After about a dozen birds, the gun jammed.
So Meredith mounted a gun on a truck. But the truck couldn't keep up, and the ride was so rough the gunner couldn't fire a single shot.
Army observers even said each pack had a leader, a tall black-feathered bird keeping watch while the others ate.
Humans incoming. Scatter!
The newspapers had a field day, and on the eighth of November the soldiers were pulled out.
But the emus kept eating, and within a week the army was back. This time, it went a bit better.
When Meredith was recalled on the tenth of December, he claimed nine hundred eighty-six kills, a figure that's highly disputed.
But his verdict on his feathered enemy became legendary.

show.text: If we had a military division with the bullet-carrying capacity of these birds it would face any army in the world… They can face machine guns with the invulnerability of tanks.
show.who: Major G.P.W. Meredith, as reported in the press

beats.say: In the end, bounties and big fences did the job the machine guns couldn't.
Final score: emus one, machine guns zero.
So there you have it: a kettle, a bucket, an ear, a very short war, a pig, and an army outrun by birds.
The lesson? People will start a war over almost anything, and sometimes the other side has feathers.
Next up: Mansa Musa, maybe the richest man who ever lived. See you there.

description:
A soup kettle, a bucket, a sailor's ear, a 38-minute war, a pig and twenty thousand emus: these are six of the most ridiculous wars in history, counted down from six to one. Some are funny, some turned deadly, and yes, one is the time the Australian army lost a fight with birds. Chapters are added automatically.
